issue_context.title: AI: ramp up cgroup v1 deprecation
issue_context.body: We should make it hard to boot in cgroupv1 mode, i.e. refuse booting unless some magic option is specified to get it anyway.
comments: Breaking boot completely when the warning delay alone would have been more than enough to raise the issue is an asshole move. There are many classes of devices where recovery is not easy, because you can't easilly edit boot arguments after system fails to boot, or because they are remote.
thanks for making me spent hours trying to debug this, really enjoyed it

> thanks for making me spent hours trying to debug this, really enjoyed it

Yeah, that's another aspect. Boot failure was completely silent in my case. Nothing in the console. After removing "quiet" kernel command line option, only extra message was message from systemd that boot was halted, no reason given. I had to add systemd debug flags to kernel command line to see some actual symptoms being reported. And the final cause of the issue was systemd itself mounting cgroup-v1 (from initramfs) and then complaining it's not supporting it (when running from rootfs) - all on Linux 6.9.

That's something to be improved, too, if this change is meant to inform users to change something, instead of just to piss them off.

> Breaking boot completely when the warning delay alone would have been more than enough to raise the issue is an asshole move. There are many classes of devices where recovery is not easy, because you can't easilly edit boot arguments after system fails to boot, or because they are remote.

Well, interestingly enough, https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/32998 has a completely different idea. Sorry, but we're deprecating a functionality here, and in such cases there's simply no way to please everyone. And the reason why we took this approach is exactly that it's noticeable by everyone yet the functionality is preserved for a while longer, giving people time to switch to cgroup v2.

We declared the deprecation initially in v253, and the NEWS file is very clear at it. It seems none of that actually helped to remind you to upgrade your setup, hence a choice must be made. If the recovery is not easy, I'd really suggest not upgrading those devices deliberately without going through changelog first.
Normal OS users don't read release notes for all SW before running pacman -Syu. Actually, I think nobody does that.

Normal OS users do not manually force the system into cgroupv1 mode either!

Please understand that support for cgroupv1 is going to go away entirely very very soon now. I think you should see the good in our slow ramp up of warnings here: we didn't completely break this for you right-away, but give you some time where we finally got you to notice that this is coming, so that you can for the moment set the kernel cmdline option, and then take your time to fix this properly by switching to cgroupv2 now.
I did not do any forcing.

It's a situation of old systemd running from initramfs using it's default config, and newer systemd from rootfs crashing the system when it stopped liking the old systemd defaults. Simple as that. The user here doesn't care about cgroups at all, let alone their versions. There were no prior warnings, because both systemds were running with default configuration, and message/30s timer *along* with an intentional crasher was added only in this change in the latest systemd version and both at once. No grace period.

Edge case of not updating initramfs often enough, I guess.

FYI I've already seen others in a similar, "we don't pay attention to cgroups/systemd release notes, just use the defaults" situation just add the `...FORCE` flag to bypass this. They will then obviously run into the problem again when cgroups v1 are removed completely; I think it would be useful to also mention here in more detail how to actually resolve the underlying issue (e.g. the commands to update initramfs via live media). I would do so myself, but I'm closer to that group of users than the ones commenting here so I wouldn't want to mislead with commands that are going to impact others' systems negatively.

initrd generation is wildly different between distributions, so this is not the right place to ask for support with that. It's something each distribution need to take care of and inform its users of.

@YHNdnzj  - Have same issue with Arch Linux ARM on an Odroid XU4 installed some time ago, but kept up to date.
The boot messages just mentioned "systemd[1]: Freezing execution.", which is very generic and didn't provide any clue to the underlying issue. Running out of options I've hooked the serial console and there I saw this: "[!!!!!!] Refusing to run under cgroup v1, SY… specified on kernel command line." which lead me to this page.

Okey, leaving this here for those interested on how to fix this on an Arch Linux, probably not the best place, but it ranks pretty up on Google, so here it goes:

I had `systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=0` added to the kernel params in boot.txt. This was done 3 or so years ago, and if I remember correctly, I've done it to make docker run.

Anyway, the fix is to edit `boot.txt`, remove the `systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=0`, run a `./mkscr` to make `boot.scr` and then reinstall the kernel with a `pacman -S linux` which will rebuild the initial ramdisk.

Interestingly enough, now docker runs without the cgroup option.

@ohnoov I ran into the same issue with the same chromebook image (I installed the image, updated, and rebooted, and ran into the issue). Is there a way to fix it now?

I've just upgraded to Fedora 41 and hit this issue. Since it was released this Monday, more people might be coming in with the same issue.

The option `systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=0` must have been set via NVIDIA Docker. Solving it is quite straightforward:

1. Press `e` in GRUB to edit the command line, remove the `systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=0` option and boot the system.
2. Edit `/etc/default/grub` and remove `systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=0` from the line with `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX`.
3. Run `sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` to generate a new config.
